original_value: AbstractA number of machine learning (ML)-based algorithms have been proposed for predicting mutation-induced stability changes in proteins. In this critical review, we used hypothetical reverse mutations to evaluate the performance of five representative algorithms and found all of them suffer from the problem of overfitting. This approach is based on the fact that if a wild-type protein is more stable than a mutant protein, then the same mutant is less stable than the wild-type protein. We analyzed the underlying issues and suggest that the main causes of the overfitting problem include that the numbers of training cases were too small, and the features used in the models were not sufficiently informative for the task. We make recommendations on how to avoid overfitting in this important research area and improve the reliability and robustness of ML-based algorithms in general.

result.paraphrase: A number of machine learning (ML)-based algorithms have been proposed to predict mutation-induced changes in protein stability. In this critical review, we used hypothetical reverse mutations to assess the performance of five representative algorithms and found that all of them suffer from overfitting. This method relies on the observation that if a wild-type protein is more stable than a mutant protein, then that mutant is less stable than the wild-type protein. We examined the underlying issues and suggest that the main causes of overfitting are too few training cases and model features that are not sufficiently informative for the task. We offer recommendations for avoiding overfitting in this important research area and for improving the reliability and robustness of ML-based algorithms in general.
